system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2127-02-15 13:12:00 to 2127-02-21 14:05:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy, and GJ tube dependence was admitted after transfer for a malfunctioning feeding tube that was displaced and likely caused aspiration pneumonia. He was stabilized, and a new GJ tube was successfully placed via interventional radiology. Nutrition was resumed, resolving mild hypoglycemia, and all chronic medications, including antiretrovirals, were restarted through the tube. His respiratory status improved to baseline, and he was discharged to extended care with instructions to maintain tube care and medication routines.
problems: Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You were brought in from your rehab facility because you were having trouble breathing and your oxygen levels were low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You’re on oxygen through your trach, and that’s helping. But we’re concerned you might have an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your white blood cell count is high, and your urine showed a lot of white blood cells. That suggests a urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and because of your history with resistant bacteria, we started strong antibiotics—vancomycin and Zosyn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were also very low on blood pressure, so we gave fluids and started a medication called norepinephrine to support it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, vasopressors. But your pressure is better now, and we’re weaning off them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray. It shows chronic lung changes, but we can’t rule out pneumonia. So we’re treating both possibilities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We took a sputum sample. It grew Pseudomonas, which is common in your case. We’ll adjust antibiotics once we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s sensitive to some drugs. But we’re watching closely. We also inserted a new IV line in your leg to give antibiotics safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back. It’s Enterococcus faecium, resistant to vancomycin—VRE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. So we’re switching to linezolid, which is effective against VRE. We’ll continue for 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum culture also confirmed Pseudomonas. It’s only intermediate to meropenem, so we’re switching to cefepime for better coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, an IV antibiotic that works well against Pseudomonas. You’ll get it every 8 hours for two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the lung opacities have increased slightly. But your oxygen needs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It could be part of your chronic lung disease. But we’re treating it as possible pneumonia, so you’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re close to your baseline. No fever, blood pressure stable, and white count is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving you out of the ICU today. You’re stable, off pressors, and improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a PICC line in your neck so you can get IV antibiotics at your facility. But the X-ray shows it’s not in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s in the internal jugular vein. It needs to be in the superior vena cava. We’ll fix that tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC was repositioned today using fluoroscopy. It’s now in the correct place in the low SVC. Good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. White count is normal, and you’re afebrile. We’re confident you can finish antibiotics at your facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely in the next two days. You’ll go home on IV cefepime, oral linezolid, and oral vancomycin for C. diff prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Cefepime for Pseudomonas pneumonia, linezolid for the VRE UTI, and vancomycin because you’ve had C. diff before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. All your chronic meds are back on—HIV drugs, seizure meds, acid reducer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, darunavir, ritonavir, Truvada—all continued. Your CD4 is 168, viral load undetectable. That’s good control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re back at your baseline. We’re discharging you to extended care with IV antibiotics for two more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get cefepime IV every 8 hours, linezolid twice daily by mouth, and vancomycin twice daily for C. diff prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And continue all your other meds—Keppra, omeprazole, atovaquone, etc. Your sister will coordinate with the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Watch for fever, increased secretions, or breathing trouble. But you’ve responded well. Great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll follow up with your primary team. They’ll monitor your labs and antibiotic course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the mend. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you shortly. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll check in soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy, and GJ tube dependence was admitted for septic shock likely from a urinary tract infection, with concern for concurrent pneumonia. He presented with hypoxia, tachycardia, and hypotension, requiring vasopressor support and ICU care. Initial treatment included broad-spectrum antibiotics, later narrowed to linezolid for VRE UTI and cefepime for Pseudomonas pneumonia based on culture results. A malpositioned PICC line was repositioned successfully. He stabilized, returned to baseline, and was discharged to extended care with a two-week course of IV cefepime, oral linezolid, and oral vancomycin, along with continuation of all chronic medications including antiretrovirals and seizure prophylaxis.
